exercises.title: Zero training error
exercises.q: You fit a degree-9 polynomial to 10 points and the training error is exactly 0. Is this a good model? What would you measure to find out?
exercises.hint: How many knobs does a degree-9 polynomial have? How many points must it pass through?
exercises.answer: Not necessarily. A degree-9 polynomial has 10 coefficients, so it can pass through any 10 points exactly. Zero training error is guaranteed, which means it tells you nothing about the pattern. Measure the error on points the model never saw (a held-out test set, or cross-validation). If test error is much larger than training error, the model memorised the noise: that gap is overfitting (Murphy §1.2.3).

exercises.title: Draw the overfitting curve yourself
exercises.q: Generate 15 noisy points from y = sin(2πx) + noise and 200 test points. Fit polynomials of degree 0 to 12 with np.polyfit. Print the train and test mean squared error for each degree and report which degree has the lowest test error.
exercises.hint: np.polyfit(x, y, d) returns coefficients; np.polyval(coef, x) evaluates them.
exercises.answer: Training error falls every time the degree goes up, because more knobs can always fit at least as well. Test error falls at first (the model can now bend like a sine), bottoms out around degree 3–6, then rises sharply as the curve starts chasing noise.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
f = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
x_tr = rng.random(15); y_tr = f(x_tr) + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 15)

    print(f"degree {d:2d}  train {tr:8.4f}  test {te:10.4f}")
    if best is None or te < best[1]:
        best = (d, te)
print("best degree on test data:", best[0])

exercises.title: Which kind of learning?
exercises.q: Name the setting (classification, regression, clustering, reinforcement) for: (a) predicting tomorrow's temperature, (b) grouping customers by shopping habits with no labels, (c) deciding if an email is spam, (d) a robot learning to walk from a reward for distance travelled.
exercises.hint: Is there a label? Is it a number or a category? Is feedback given per step or only as a reward?
exercises.answer: (a) Regression: the target is a number. (b) Clustering: no labels, find groups. (c) Classification: the label is one of two categories. (d) Reinforcement learning: no correct action is given, only a reward signal that may arrive late.

exercises.title: The COVID test by hand
exercises.q: A test has sensitivity P(+|sick) = 0.875 and specificity P(−|healthy) = 0.975. In a population where 10% are infected, what is P(sick | +)? Repeat for 1% infected.
exercises.hint: P(+) = P(+|sick)P(sick) + P(+|healthy)P(healthy), and P(+|healthy) = 1 − specificity.
exercises.answer: With 10%: numerator = 0.875 × 0.1 = 0.0875. False positives = 0.025 × 0.9 = 0.0225. P(+) = 0.0875 + 0.0225 = 0.11. P(sick|+) = 0.0875 / 0.11 ≈ 0.795. With 1%: numerator = 0.00875, false positives = 0.025 × 0.99 = 0.02475, P(+) = 0.0335, P(sick|+) ≈ 0.261. Same test, very different meaning: when the disease is rare, most positives come from the large healthy group (Murphy §2.3.1).

import numpy as np
z = np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    naive = np.exp(z) / np.exp(z).sum()
print("naive :", naive)

def softmax(z):
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())  # subtract the largest score before exponentiating
    return e / e.sum()

def logsumexp(z):
    m = z.max()
    return m + np.log(np.exp(z - m).sum())  # pull the max out of the log
print("stable:", softmax(z).round(3))
print("logsumexp:", round(logsumexp(z), 4))

exercises.title: Why σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z))
exercises.q: Differentiate σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^−z) and show the result can be written as σ(z)(1 − σ(z)).
exercises.hint: Write σ = (1 + e^−z)^−1 and use the chain rule. Then notice 1 − σ = e^−z / (1 + e^−z).
exercises.answer: σ′(z) = −(1 + e^−z)^−2 · (−e^−z) = e^−z / (1 + e^−z)². Split it: [1 / (1 + e^−z)] · [e^−z / (1 + e^−z)] = σ(z) · (1 − σ(z)), because 1 − σ = (1 + e^−z − 1)/(1 + e^−z) = e^−z/(1 + e^−z). So the slope can be computed from the output alone, which is why backprop through a sigmoid is cheap (station 4).

exercises.title: Covariance by hand, and a trap
exercises.q: (a) For x = [1,2,3,4,5] and y = [2,4,5,4,5], compute the covariance and correlation by hand in NumPy and check against np.cov / np.corrcoef. (b) Let x be 10,000 standard normals and y = x². Show the correlation is ≈ 0 even though y is a function of x.
exercises.hint: cov = mean((x − x̄)(y − ȳ)); np.cov uses n − 1 in the denominator by default.
exercises.answer: (a) Covariance (n − 1 version) = 1.5, correlation ≈ 0.775. (b) Correlation ≈ 0, because for every positive x there's a matching negative x with the same y, so the linear trend cancels. Correlation only measures straight-line relationships; zero correlation does not mean independence (Murphy §3.1.3).

exercises.title: Condition a 2-D Gaussian
exercises.q: Heights and weights are jointly Gaussian with μ_h = 170 cm, σ_h = 10, μ_w = 70 kg, σ_w = 12, correlation ρ = 0.6. What are the mean and standard deviation of weight for someone 190 cm tall?
exercises.hint: E[w|h] = μ_w + ρ(σ_w/σ_h)(h − μ_h);  Var[w|h] = σ_w²(1 − ρ²).
exercises.answer: E[w | h=190] = 70 + 0.6 × (12/10) × 20 = 70 + 14.4 = 84.4 kg. Var = 144 × (1 − 0.36) = 92.16, so σ ≈ 9.6 kg. Knowing the height shifts your guess and makes you more certain (12 → 9.6 kg). Murphy §3.2.3.

exercises.title: Simpson's paradox in one table
exercises.q: Treatment A cures 81/87 small stones and 192/263 large stones. Treatment B cures 234/270 small and 55/80 large. Which is better within each group? Which looks better overall? Why?
exercises.hint: Compute four percentages, then the two overall percentages. Who got the hard cases?
exercises.answer: Small: A 93% vs B 87%. Large: A 73% vs B 69%. A wins in both groups. Overall: A 273/350 = 78%, B 289/350 = 83%, so B looks better. The reversal happens because A was given most of the hard (large-stone) cases. The group variable confounds the comparison; you have to condition on it (Murphy §3.1.5).

exercises.title: The coin's MLE from scratch
exercises.q: You flip a coin n times and see h heads. Write the log-likelihood of θ and find the θ that maximises it.
exercises.hint: log L = h log θ + (n − h) log(1 − θ). Set its derivative to zero.
exercises.answer: d/dθ log L = h/θ − (n − h)/(1 − θ) = 0 ⇒ h(1 − θ) = (n − h)θ ⇒ h = nθ ⇒ θ̂ = h/n. The second derivative, −h/θ² − (n−h)/(1−θ)², is negative, so it's a maximum. The 'obvious' answer, heads over flips, is exactly what maximum likelihood gives (Murphy §4.2.3).

exercises.title: The MLE of variance is biased
exercises.q: Draw 100,000 samples of size n = 5 from N(0, 4). For each, compute the MLE variance (divide by n) and the unbiased version (divide by n − 1). Average each over all samples and compare with the true 4.
exercises.hint: x.var(axis=1, ddof=0) vs ddof=1.
exercises.answer: The MLE averages ≈ 3.2 = 4 × (n−1)/n: it underestimates, because measuring spread around the sample mean (which sits in the middle of your own points) always looks tighter than around the true mean. Dividing by n − 1 corrects this and averages ≈ 4.

exercises.q: Fit a degree-12 polynomial to 15 noisy sine points with ridge regression w = (ΦᵀΦ + λI)⁻¹Φᵀy, for λ = 0, 1e−6, 1e−3, 1. Print the largest |weight| and the test error for each.

exercises.title: The cost-optimal threshold
exercises.q: A false negative costs c_FN and a false positive costs c_FP. Given p = P(y = 1 | x), when should you predict 1? Work out the threshold for c_FN = 9, c_FP = 1.
exercises.hint: Expected cost of predicting 1 is (1 − p)·c_FP; of predicting 0 is p·c_FN.
exercises.answer: Predict 1 when (1 − p)c_FP < p·c_FN ⇔ p > c_FP / (c_FP + c_FN). With c_FN = 9 and c_FP = 1, the threshold is 1/10 = 0.1: if missing a positive is 9× worse, you flag anything with more than a 10% chance. 0.5 is only right when the costs are equal (Murphy §5.1.2).

exercises.title: What a p-value is not
exercises.q: A study reports p = 0.03 for 'the drug works'. Which statements are true? (a) There's a 3% chance the drug doesn't work. (b) If the drug did nothing, results at least this extreme would happen about 3% of the time. (c) The effect is large. (d) There's a 97% chance the result will replicate.
exercises.hint: A p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true.
exercises.answer: Only (b). A p-value is P(data at least this extreme | no effect). It isn't P(no effect | data); that would need a prior, i.e. Bayes' rule. It says nothing about effect size, and doesn't give a replication probability (Murphy §5.5.4).

exercises.title: Entropy, cross-entropy, KL

exercises.hint: Use np.log2. KL = Σ p log(p/q).
exercises.answer: H(p) ≈ 1.357 bits and H(p, q) = 2 bits (a uniform code over 4 outcomes always costs 2 bits), so KL(p‖q) ≈ 0.643 = 2 − 1.357. Swapping the arguments gives KL(q‖p) ≈ 0.620: a different number. KL is not a distance, so which distribution is 'the truth' matters (Murphy §6.2.6).

import numpy as np
def H(p):       return -np.sum(p * np.log2(p))  # average surprise
def CE(p, q):   return -np.sum(p * np.log2(q))  # surprise of p's outcomes under q
def KL(p, q):   return np.sum(p * np.log2(p / q))  # extra surprise

exercises.title: KL between two coins
exercises.q: Compute KL(p‖q) in bits for two coins with P(heads) = 0.9 and 0.5. Then explain why KL can never be negative.
exercises.answer: 0.9 × log₂ 1.8 + 0.1 × log₂ 0.2 = 0.9 × 0.848 + 0.1 × (−2.322) = 0.763 − 0.232 = 0.531 bits. Non-negativity: −KL = Σ p log(q/p) ≤ log Σ p (q/p) = log Σ q = log 1 = 0, by Jensen's inequality (log is concave, so the average of logs ≤ log of the average). Equality only when q = p (Murphy §6.2.4).

exercises.title: Why classifiers minimise cross-entropy
exercises.q: Training a classifier minimises the average −log q(true label). Explain in two sentences why this is the same as making the model's distribution q match the data's distribution p.
exercises.hint: Cross-entropy = entropy + KL. Which part can the model change?
exercises.answer: The average −log q over the data is the cross-entropy H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p‖q). H(p) depends only on the data, so the only part training can lower is KL(p‖q), which is zero exactly when q = p. That's also maximum likelihood (Murphy §6.2.5).

exercises.title: Gradient of the squared error
exercises.q: Show that the gradient of f(w) = ‖Xw − y‖² is 2Xᵀ(Xw − y), and set it to zero to get the normal equations.
exercises.hint: Write f = (Xw − y)ᵀ(Xw − y) = wᵀXᵀXw − 2yᵀXw + yᵀy, then use ∇(wᵀAw) = (A + Aᵀ)w and ∇(bᵀw) = b.
exercises.answer: ∇f = (XᵀX + (XᵀX)ᵀ)w − 2Xᵀy = 2XᵀXw − 2Xᵀy = 2Xᵀ(Xw − y). Setting it to 0: XᵀXw = Xᵀy, so ŵ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy when XᵀX is invertible. Geometrically, the residual Xw − y must be perpendicular to every column of X (Murphy §7.7.3, §11.2.2).

exercises.title: Three ways to solve least squares
exercises.q: With X random 100×3 and y = X[1, −2, 0.5] + noise, solve for w with (a) the normal equations, (b) np.linalg.lstsq, (c) the pseudo-inverse. Then make two columns nearly identical and compare the condition number and the answers.

exercises.answer: On well-conditioned data all three agree to 3 decimals. With two nearly identical columns the problem itself is ill-posed: the data only pins down the sum of their two weights (≈ 1), so every method returns huge weights of opposite sign that cancel. The normal equations also disagree with the others from the 4th digit on, because forming XᵀX squares the condition number and throws away precision. The real fix is to change the problem: ridge (a small λ makes the weights small and stable) or dropping one of the duplicate columns.

exercises.title: Newton's method by hand
exercises.q: Minimise f(x) = x⁴ − 3x² + 2 with Newton's method starting at x₀ = 2. Do two steps by hand.
exercises.hint: x ← x − f′(x)/f″(x), with f′ = 4x³ − 6x and f″ = 12x² − 6.
exercises.answer: x₀ = 2: f′ = 32 − 12 = 20, f″ = 48 − 6 = 42, x₁ = 2 − 20/42 ≈ 1.524. x₁: f′ = 4(3.540) − 9.143 ≈ 5.016, f″ = 12(2.322) − 6 ≈ 21.87, x₂ ≈ 1.524 − 0.229 ≈ 1.294. The true minimum is √1.5 ≈ 1.225, and Newton converges quadratically: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step once close.

exercises.title: Naive Bayes spam filter from scratch
exercises.q: Train a naive Bayes classifier on six tiny emails (3 spam, 3 ham) using word counts with add-one (Laplace) smoothing. Classify 'win money now' and 'meeting tomorrow'. Print the log-odds for each.
exercises.hint: log P(spam | words) ∝ log P(spam) + Σ_w log P(w | spam). With add-one smoothing, P(w | c) = (count + 1) / (total words in c + vocabulary size).
exercises.answer: 'win money now' gets a large positive log-odds (spam), 'meeting tomorrow' a negative one (ham). 'Naive' means each word is treated as independent given the class, so the probabilities multiply (logs add). Add-one smoothing stops an unseen word from giving probability 0, which would wipe out everything else (Murphy §9.3.2–9.3.3).

exercises.title: Why a shared covariance gives a straight boundary
exercises.q: Two classes are Gaussian with means μ₀, μ₁ and the same covariance Σ. Show that log p(x|1) − log p(x|0) is linear in x.
exercises.hint: Expand −½(x − μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x − μ) = −½xᵀΣ⁻¹x + μᵀΣ⁻¹x − ½μᵀΣ⁻¹μ for each class and subtract.
exercises.answer: Both classes contribute the same −½xᵀΣ⁻¹x term (same Σ), and it cancels in the difference. What remains is (μ₁ − μ₀)ᵀΣ⁻¹x + constant: a weighted sum of x plus a bias. So the log-odds is wᵀx + b with w = Σ⁻¹(μ₁ − μ₀). That's exactly logistic regression's form (Murphy §9.2.3). With different covariances the quadratic terms don't cancel and the boundary curves (QDA).

exercises.title: Logistic regression is convex
exercises.q: For NLL(w) = −Σ [yₙ log μₙ + (1 − yₙ) log(1 − μₙ)] with μₙ = σ(wᵀxₙ), show the gradient is Σ(μₙ − yₙ)xₙ and the Hessian is Σ μₙ(1 − μₙ) xₙxₙᵀ. Why does that make the loss convex?
exercises.hint: Use dμ/dz = μ(1 − μ) (exercise 2.5) and the chain rule.
exercises.answer: d/dz of −[y log μ + (1−y) log(1−μ)] = −[y(1−μ) − (1−y)μ] = μ − y; times dz/dw = x gives (μ − y)x. Differentiating again: d(μ − y)/dw = μ(1−μ)x, so H = Σ μ(1−μ) x xᵀ. For any vector v, vᵀHv = Σ μ(1−μ)(vᵀx)² ≥ 0 because μ(1−μ) > 0. A Hessian that's never negative means the bowl curves upward in every direction: one global minimum and no traps (Murphy §10.2.3.4).

exercises.title: What ridge does to each direction
exercises.q: Using the SVD X = USVᵀ, show that ridge predictions are ŷ = Σⱼ uⱼ · sⱼ²/(sⱼ² + λ) · uⱼᵀy. Which directions get shrunk most?
exercises.hint: ŵ = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy. Substitute XᵀX = VS²Vᵀ.
exercises.answer: (VS²Vᵀ + λI)⁻¹ = V(S² + λI)⁻¹Vᵀ, so ŵ = V(S² + λI)⁻¹SUᵀy and ŷ = Xŵ = US(S² + λI)⁻¹SUᵀy = Σ uⱼ [sⱼ²/(sⱼ²+λ)] uⱼᵀy. Least squares keeps every direction fully (factor 1). Ridge multiplies each by sⱼ²/(sⱼ²+λ): directions with large singular values (where the data varies a lot) barely shrink, while small-variance directions, the noisy ones, shrink toward 0. That's 'soft PCA' (Murphy §11.3.2).

exercises.title: Pick the GLM
exercises.q: Which output distribution and link would you use for: (a) house price, (b) whether a customer churns, (c) number of insurance claims per year, (d) which of 5 products a user clicks?
exercises.hint: Match the distribution to what the target can be: any real number, yes/no, a count, one of K.
exercises.answer: (a) Gaussian with identity link: linear regression. (b) Bernoulli with logit link: logistic regression. (c) Poisson with log link, so the predicted rate is always positive. (d) Categorical with softmax: multinomial logistic regression. Same recipe each time: a linear score, then the squash that suits the output type (Murphy §12.2).

That's non-convexity (ch. 8) in its smallest form: about half of random starts fail with only 2 hidden units. Fixes: more hidden units (more ways downhill) or several random restarts (Murphy §13.2.1).

exercises.title: Backprop for one hidden layer, in matrices
exercises.q: For h = ReLU(XW₁ + b₁), ŷ = hW₂ + b₂, L = ‖ŷ − Y‖²/(2N), derive ∂L/∂W₂, ∂L/∂h, ∂L/∂W₁. Check that the shapes match.
exercises.hint: Start from ∂L/∂ŷ = (ŷ − Y)/N and use station 4's rules: multiply passes blame by the other input; ReLU passes it only where the unit was on.
exercises.answer: δ₂ = ∂L/∂ŷ = (ŷ − Y)/N (N×K). ∂L/∂W₂ = hᵀδ₂ (H×K, matches W₂). ∂L/∂b₂ = Σ rows of δ₂. ∂L/∂h = δ₂W₂ᵀ (N×H). Through ReLU: δ₁ = (δ₂W₂ᵀ) ⊙ 𝟙(XW₁ + b₁ > 0). ∂L/∂W₁ = Xᵀδ₁ (D×H, matches W₁). Every weight gradient is (input to that layer)ᵀ × (blame at its output), which is the matrix version of 'times the other input' (Murphy §13.3.2).

import numpy as np
x = np.zeros((8, 8)); x[:, 4:] = 1.0
K = np.array([[-1, 0, 1]] * 3, dtype=float)
def conv2d(x, K):
    k = K.shape[0]; out = np.zeros((x.shape[0] - k + 1, x.shape[1] - k + 1))
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        for j in range(out.shape[1]):
            out[i, j] = np.sum(x[i:i + k, j:j + k] * K)  # one dot product per position
    return out
def maxpool(x):
    H, W = x.shape[0] // 2, x.shape[1] // 2
    return x[:2 * H, :2 * W].reshape(H, 2, W, 2).max(axis=(1, 3))  # max over each 2x2 block
y = conv2d(x, K)
fast = np.einsum("ijkl,kl->ij", np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(x, (3, 3)), K)
print("conv output row 0:", y[0]); print("loops == vectorised:", np.allclose(y, fast))
print("after 2x2 max-pool:\n", maxpool(y))

exercises.title: Count the weights
exercises.q: A 32×32 RGB image goes into (a) a fully connected layer with 1,024 outputs, (b) a conv layer with 64 filters of size 3×3. How many weights (ignore biases) does each have, and how many outputs?
exercises.hint: Dense: inputs × outputs. Conv: k × k × in_channels × out_channels.
exercises.answer: (a) 32·32·3 = 3,072 inputs × 1,024 = 3,145,728 weights, 1,024 outputs. (b) 3·3·3·64 = 1,728 weights, and with 'same' padding 32·32·64 = 65,536 outputs. The conv layer has about 1,800× fewer weights yet 64× more outputs, because the same 1,728 numbers are reused at every position (Murphy §14.2.1).

exercises.title: Why residual connections help, measured
exercises.q: Build a 50-layer ReLU network (width 64, weights with std 1/√n) with and without residual connections x ← x + 0.1·ReLU(Wx). Backpropagate a unit gradient and compare its norm at layer 1.
exercises.hint: Without a skip the layer Jacobian is W·diag(mask); with one it is I + 0.1·W·diag(mask).
exercises.answer: Without skips the gradient shrinks to about 10⁻⁸: each ReLU layer switches off about half the units, so with std 1/√n each layer roughly halves the gradient's energy, and 50 layers compound that. With skips each Jacobian is I + (small term), so there's always a direct identity path back and the gradient arrives with a healthy size (≈ 5). That's why ResNets can be hundreds of layers deep (Murphy §13.4.4, §14.3.4).

exercises.title: Why dividing by √d keeps softmax gradients alive
exercises.q: Suppose q and k have independent entries with mean 0 and variance 1. Find the mean and variance of q·k in dimension d, and explain what happens to the softmax Jacobian ∂softmax(z)/∂z when d = 512 without the 1/√d scale.
exercises.hint: Var(Σᵢ qᵢ kᵢ) = Σᵢ Var(qᵢ kᵢ), and for independent mean-zero variables Var(qᵢ kᵢ) = Var(qᵢ)Var(kᵢ) = 1.
exercises.answer: Each product qᵢkᵢ has mean 0 and variance 1, so the sum of d independent terms q·k has mean 0 and variance d (standard deviation √d). At d = 512, typical dot products are ±22.6; feeding ±22.6 into exp() makes the largest score take probability α_max ≈ 1 − 10⁻¹⁰ and all others ≈ 0, where the softmax gradient αᵢ(1 − αᵢ) vanishes. Dividing by √d restores unit variance regardless of d (Murphy §15.4.2).

exercises.title: Gaussian process regression posterior from scratch
exercises.q: Observe 6 noisy points from y = sin(x) on [−2.5, 2.5] with noise σ = 0.1. Using the RBF kernel k(x, x′) = exp(−(x − x′)² / (2ℓ²)) with ℓ = 1.0, compute the exact GP posterior mean μ* and standard deviation σ* at a test point x* = 0.0 (surrounded by data) and at x* = 4.5 (far outside the data).
exercises.hint: Solve (K + σ²I) α = y; then μ* = k*ᵀ α and σ*² = k(x*, x*) − k*ᵀ (K + σ²I)⁻¹ k*.
exercises.answer: At x* = 0.0 (surrounded by training points) the posterior uncertainty is tiny (σ* ≈ 0.06), whereas at x* = 4.5 (far from data) the mean reverts toward 0 and the posterior std balloons back to nearly the full prior std 1.0 (σ* ≈ 0.996). That automatic 'I don't know far from data' is why GPs power Bayesian optimisation (Murphy §17.2, D2L ch. 18).

x* =  0.0: posterior mean = -0.001,  posterior std = 0.103
x* =  4.5: posterior mean = +0.021,  posterior std = 0.992

import numpy as np
X = np.array([-2.2, -1.3, -0.4, 0.5, 1.4, 2.3])
y = np.sin(X)
ell, sig = 1.0, 0.1
rbf = lambda a, b: np.exp(-0.5 * (a[:, None] - b[None, :])**2 / ell**2)
K = rbf(X, X) + (sig**2) * np.eye(len(X))
X_test = np.array([0.0, 4.5])
K_s = rbf(X_test, X)
mu = K_s @ np.linalg.solve(K, y)  # posterior mean k*ᵀ (K + σ²I)⁻¹ y
var = 1.0 - np.sum(K_s * np.linalg.solve(K, K_s.T).T, axis=1)  # posterior variance
for x0, m, s in zip(X_test, mu, np.sqrt(var)):
    print(f"x* = {x0:4.1f}: posterior mean = {m:+.3f},  posterior std = {s:.3f}")

import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 40); y = x ** 2
F = np.full_like(y, y.mean()); lr = 0.3
for m in range(1, 26):
    r = y - F  # negative gradient of ½(y - F)²

    F += lr * stump  # additive boosting update

exercises.title: LoRA: low-rank adaptation from scratch
exercises.q: Suppose a pretrained layer W₀ ∈ ℝ^{64×64} is frozen, and the true target weight matrix differs by a rank-2 perturbation ΔW* = B* A*. Train only a rank-r = 2 LoRA adapter B ∈ ℝ^{64×2}, A ∈ ℝ^{2×64} (256 parameters instead of 4,096) by gradient descent on ‖X(W₀ + BA) − Y‖²/(2N). Print the parameter savings and final MSE.
exercises.hint: Initialize A ~ N(0, 0.1) and B = 0 so W₀ + BA starts at exact W₀; gradient for B is (Xᵀ err) Aᵀ and for A is Bᵀ (Xᵀ err).
exercises.answer: Training just 256 LoRA weights (6.25% of the 4,096 frozen weights in W₀) drives the adaptation error down to ~10⁻⁶, while starting from B = 0 guarantees that step 0 preserves the pretrained model's exact behaviour (Murphy §19.2).

exercises.solution:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
d, r, N = 64, 2, 120
W0 = rng.normal(0, 1 / np.sqrt(d), (d, d))
W_star = W0 + rng.normal(0, 0.2, (d, r)) @ rng.normal(0, 0.2, (r, d))
X = rng.normal(size=(N, d)); Y = X @ W_star
A = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (d, r)); B = np.zeros((r, d))  # B=0 so adapter starts as exact zero
for step in range(400):
    err = (X @ (W0 + A @ B) - Y) / N
    gW = X.T @ err
    A, B = A - 0.5 * (gW @ B.T), B - 0.5 * (A.T @ gW)  # low-rank chain-rule gradients
print(f"trainable params: {A.size + B.size} / {W0.size} ({100*(A.size+B.size)/W0.size:.1f}%)")
print(f"initial MSE: {np.mean((X @ W0 - Y)**2):.4f}  ->  LoRA MSE: {np.mean((X @ (W0 + A @ B) - Y)**2):.6f}")

exercises.title: Linear autoencoder vs PCA subspace equivalence
exercises.q: Generate N = 200 points in ℝ⁵ with different variances along each axis. Compare the reconstruction MSE of (a) exact rank-2 PCA via SVD, and (b) a 5 → 2 → 5 linear autoencoder X W₁ W₂ trained by gradient descent.

exercises.title: K-means clustering & monotonic distortion drop
exercises.q: Generate 3 isotropic 2-D clusters (150 points total) and run Lloyd's K-means loop for 8 iterations from 3 random points as initial centroids. Print the distortion J = (1/N) Σₙ ‖xₙ − μ_{cₙ}‖² at each step and verify it never increases.

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
X = np.vstack([rng.normal([-2, 0], 0.5, (50, 2)), rng.normal([2, 0], 0.5, (50, 2)), rng.normal([0, 2.5], 0.5, (50, 2))])

exercises.q: Minimise the anisotropic bowl f(x₁, x₂) = 0.5 x₁² + 50 x₂² (condition number κ = 100) starting from (4, 4) for 60 steps using (a) plain GD with η = 0.018, and (b) Adam with η = 0.25, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999. Compare the final loss.

projects.title: Regression from scratch on real medical data
projects.blurb: Predict disease progression from 10 patient measurements (scikit-learn's diabetes dataset, 442 patients, bundled with Colab). You'll build linear regression four ways (closed form, gradient descent, ridge with cross-validation) and put an honest error bar on one coefficient with the bootstrap. Uses Murphy ch. 4, 5, 7, 8 and 11.

tr, te = idx[:cut], idx[cut:]
mu, sd = X[tr].mean(0), X[tr].std(0)

ytr, yte = y[tr], y[te]

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
d = load_diabetes()
X, y, names = d.data, d.target, d.feature_names
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng.permutation(len(y)); cut = int(0.8 * len(y))
tr, te = idx[:cut], idx[cut:]
mu, sd = X[tr].mean(0), X[tr].std(0)
Xtr = (X[tr] - mu) / sd  # standardise with TRAINING statistics
Xte = (X[te] - mu) / sd  # same transform for the test set
ytr, yte = y[tr], y[te]
print(Xtr.shape, Xte.shape, names)

steps.title: Closed-form least squares
steps.q: Add a column of ones for the bias and solve the normal equations. Report the test MSE and R² (1 − MSE / variance of y). Which feature has the largest weight?
steps.answer: The normal equations give the exact minimum of the squared error in one step (Murphy §11.2). Test R² ≈ 0.35 on this split: the 10 measurements explain about a third of the variation in disease progression (other splits give up to ≈ 0.5). BMI and s5 get the largest positive weights; s1 gets a large negative one that partly cancels its correlated twin s2. Because features are standardised, weight sizes are comparable.

A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xtr)), Xtr])
w = ...  # TODO: normal equations (X^T X) w = X^T y
pred = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xte)), Xte]) @ w
mse = np.mean((pred - yte) ** 2)
print(f"test MSE {mse:.1f}   R^2 {1 - mse / yte.var():.3f}")
print("largest weight:", names[np.argmax(np.abs(w[1:]))], np.round(w[1:], 1))
steps.solution:
A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xtr)), Xtr])
w = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ ytr)  # normal equations (X^T X) w = X^T y
pred = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xte)), Xte]) @ w
mse = np.mean((pred - yte) ** 2)
print(f"test MSE {mse:.1f}   R^2 {1 - mse / yte.var():.3f}")
print("largest weight:", names[np.argmax(np.abs(w[1:]))], np.round(w[1:], 1))

steps.title: The same answer by gradient descent
steps.q: Minimise the mean squared error with plain gradient descent (learning rate 0.1, 2,000 steps) starting from zeros. Compare the weights with the closed form.
steps.answer: Most weights match, but the largest gap is still ≈ 0.7 after 2,000 steps. The culprit is s1 and s2: they are strongly correlated, which turns the bowl into a long, flat valley (an ill-conditioned problem, Murphy §8.2.3), and gradient descent crawls along it. The loss is convex, so it will get there; run 20,000 steps and watch the gap shrink. This slow-valley effect is exactly what momentum and Adam fix.
steps.starter:
wg = np.zeros(A.shape[1])
for step in range(2000):
    grad = ...  # TODO: gradient of the mean squared error
    wg -= 0.1 * grad
print("max |w_gd - w_closed| =", np.abs(wg - w).max().round(4))
steps.solution:
wg = np.zeros(A.shape[1])
for step in range(2000):
    grad = 2 * A.T @ (A @ wg - ytr) / len(ytr)  # gradient of the mean squared error
    wg -= 0.1 * grad
print("max |w_gd - w_closed| =", np.abs(wg - w).max().round(4))

steps.title: Ridge with 5-fold cross-validation
steps.q: For λ in a log grid from 1e−3 to 1e3, fit ridge (don't penalise the bias) and measure 5-fold CV error on the training set. Pick the best λ, refit on all training data, report test MSE.
steps.answer: Small λ ≈ ordinary least squares; huge λ shrinks every weight to zero and underfits. The CV curve is fairly flat for small λ here because 10 features and 353 patients isn't a hard overfitting problem, and the best λ gives a test MSE close to plain least squares. Ridge helps most when features are many or correlated (s1 and s2 are highly correlated here).

def ridge(A, y, lam):
    P = lam * np.eye(A.shape[1]); P[0, 0] = 0            # don't penalise the bias
    return ...  # TODO: ridge closed form
folds = np.array_split(np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(len(ytr)), 5)
lams = np.logspace(-3, 3, 13); cv = []
for lam in lams:
    errs = []
    for k in range(5):
        v = folds[k]; t = np.concatenate([folds[j] for j in range(5) if j != k])
        wr = ridge(A[t], ytr[t], lam)
        errs.append(np.mean((A[v] @ wr - ytr[v]) ** 2))
    cv.append(np.mean(errs))
best = lams[int(np.argmin(cv))]
wr = ridge(A, ytr, best)
print("CV errors:", np.round(cv, 0))
print(f"best lambda {best:.3g}  test MSE {np.mean((np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xte)), Xte]) @ wr - yte)**2):.1f}")
steps.solution:
def ridge(A, y, lam):
    P = lam * np.eye(A.shape[1]); P[0, 0] = 0            # don't penalise the bias
    return np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + P, A.T @ y)  # ridge closed form
folds = np.array_split(np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(len(ytr)), 5)
lams = np.logspace(-3, 3, 13); cv = []
for lam in lams:

        wr = ridge(A[t], ytr[t], lam)
        errs.append(np.mean((A[v] @ wr - ytr[v]) ** 2))
    cv.append(np.mean(errs))
best = lams[int(np.argmin(cv))]
wr = ridge(A, ytr, best)
print("CV errors:", np.round(cv, 0))
print(f"best lambda {best:.3g}  test MSE {np.mean((np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xte)), Xte]) @ wr - yte)**2):.1f}")

steps.title: Write-up
steps.q: In four sentences: what did each method add, and which model would you deploy?
steps.answer: Closed form gives the exact least-squares answer instantly; gradient descent reaches the same answer by a method that also works when no formula exists; ridge plus cross-validation chose how much to shrink using only training data; the bootstrap measured how much a coefficient would wobble with new patients. Deploy ridge with the CV-chosen λ (here nearly identical to least squares), report its test MSE, and report the bootstrap interval for any coefficient you interpret.

steps.title: What the numbers do and don't say
steps.q: Your manager reads step 4 and says: 'p = 0.03, so there's a 97% chance B is better.' Correct the sentence, then say which of your results actually answers the manager's question.
steps.answer: A p-value is P(data at least this extreme | no difference). It is not P(no difference | data), and 1 − p is not the chance that B is better: that's the prosecutor's fallacy (Murphy §5.5.4). The quantity the manager wants, P(B better | data), is the Bayesian posterior probability from step 5. With a flat prior and this much data it happens to be close to 1 − p/2, but in general it depends on the prior, and the two numbers answer different questions. Also say how big the effect is (the interval from steps 2–3), not just whether it's 'significant'. And only quote a p-value if you decided the sample size in advance: step 7 shows that peeking inflates false positives far above 5%.

steps.title: Gaussian naive Bayes from scratch
steps.q: Fit one mean and one variance per feature per class, plus the class prior. Score a point by log prior + Σ log N(xⱼ | μ, σ²), and turn the two scores into P(malignant | x) with a softmax. Report test accuracy.
steps.answer: Naive Bayes gets ≈ 90% test accuracy, well above the 63% baseline, but it's the weakest of the three. The 30 features come in families (radius, perimeter and area of the same cell are nearly the same measurement), so the 'independent given the class' assumption is badly wrong: naive Bayes counts the same evidence three times (Murphy §9.3).

steps.title: LDA from scratch

steps.answer: LDA gets ≈ 94%. Modelling the correlations between features with a full shared covariance removes naive Bayes' double counting. The boundary is still a straight line (a weighted sum of features), with weights w = Σ⁻¹(μ₁ − μ₀): Σ⁻¹ down-weights features that are redundant with others (Murphy §9.2).

def kmeans(X, k, seed):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed); C = X[r.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]

        lab = np.argmin(((X[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(2), 1)  # nearest centre

    return lab, C, ((X - C[lab]) ** 2).sum()
runs = [kmeans(X, 3, s) for s in range(10)]

steps.title: Backward pass and a gradient check
steps.q: Send the blame back: softmax+cross-entropy gives (p − y)/N, then dense, then un-pool (the gradient goes only to the max position), then ReLU (zero where z ≤ 0), then the conv weights (colsᵀ · gradient). Check a few weights of each parameter against finite differences.

(2) The conv bias starts at 0.01 rather than 0, so blank background pixels don't sit exactly on ReLU's kink, where the derivative is undefined and finite differences disagree with any choice you make. steps.title: An associative lookup task that needs attention
steps.q: Create sequences of 5 tokens: two key-value pairs (k1, v1, k2, v2) followed by a query key q ∈ {k1, k2}, where keys are in {0..3} and values are in {4..7}. The target is the value paired with q. Generate 1,200 training and 300 test sequences.
steps.answer: Each sequence [k1, v1, k2, v2, q] contains the exact same bag of tokens whether q = k1 or q = k2 (only the last token changes, and the answer depends on which earlier position matches q and reading its right-hand neighbour). A bag-of-words model that averages token embeddings cannot tell which value belongs to which key; an attention head that looks from position 4 (q) to position 0 or 2 and reads the adjacent value solves it cleanly.
steps.starter:
import numpy as np

    sc = (Q[:, -1:, :] @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1))[:, 0, :] / np.sqrt(D)  # query t=4 attends to t=0..4
    sc -= sc.max(1, keepdims=True); A = np.exp(sc); A /= A.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    c = (A[:, :, None] * Vv).sum(1)  # attended context (N, D)
    logits = c @ P["WO"] + P["b"]
    logits -= logits.max(1, keepdims=True); p = np.exp(logits); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)

    dH[:, -1, :] += dQ_last @ P["WQ"].T
